title: Heavy-Light Decomposition (Path Queries)
directAnswer: Heavy-light decomposition (HLD) makes path queries on a tree fast. Each node picks its child with the largest subtree as its 'heavy' child; the heavy edges link nodes into chains. Lay the chains out contiguously in an array (via DFS position) and back that array with a segment tree. Any root-to-node path crosses at most O(log n) chains, so a path query splits into O(log n) contiguous segment-tree ranges — giving O(log^2 n) per path query (O(log n) chains × O(log n) per range).

remember.pattern: Heavy child = biggest subtree; chains laid contiguously; path = O(log n) chain ranges
remember.formula:
heavy[node] = child with max subtree size
# DFS 1: subtree sizes + heavy child
# DFS 2: assign pos[node] along chains; head[node] = chain top
query(u, v):
  res = identity
  while head[u] != head[v]:
    if depth[head[u]] < depth[head[v]]: swap(u, v)
    res = combine(res, seg.query(pos[head[u]], pos[u]))
    u = parent[head[u]]
  # now same chain: combine the final in-chain range
  if depth[u] > depth[v]: swap(u, v)
  res = combine(res, seg.query(pos[u], pos[v]))
rules: **Heavy child** = the child whose subtree is largest; ties broken arbitrarily. Every other child starts a new (light) chain.
A light edge at least **halves** the subtree size going down, so any root-to-leaf path has at most **log2 n light edges** → O(log n) chains.
Lay each chain **contiguously** in the base array so a chain segment is one segment-tree range.
**head[node]** is the topmost node of node's chain; jump `u = parent[head[u]]` to hop to the next chain up.
Climb the **deeper head** each step (compare depth[head[u]] vs depth[head[v]]) — this is implicitly walking toward the LCA.
whenToUse: Path queries/updates between two nodes (sum, max, add) on a static-shape tree
Mixing path aggregates with subtree aggregates (HLD orders nodes so both are ranges)
Repeated 'value on the path from u to v' questions where naive walking is too slow
When you already know segment trees and need to lift them to tree paths
antiSignals: Only subtree queries, no paths → a plain Euler tour + Fenwick tree is simpler
Only LCA / distance, no aggregates → binary lifting is shorter
Tree changes shape between queries → link-cut trees handle dynamic trees instead
A single path query → just walk it in O(n); HLD's setup is not worth it
remember.takeaway: HLD is the bridge from 'range structure on an array' to 'range structure on tree paths'. By choosing heavy edges so light edges are rare (≤ log n on any path), it guarantees every path is a small union of contiguous chain ranges — letting a segment tree answer path queries in O(log^2 n).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand why choosing the largest-subtree child bounds light edges at O(log n), and how that turns a path into O(log n) contiguous ranges a segment tree can answer.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Picking the heavy child by depth or degree instead of subtree size (losing the log bound), laying chains non-contiguously, or mishandling the final same-chain segment (forgetting to include the right endpoint or double-counting the LCA on edge-valued trees).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the O(log n) light-edge bound from the halving argument, describe the two-DFS build crisply, and contrast HLD (paths, O(log^2 n)) with Euler tour (subtrees, O(log n)) and binary lifting (LCA only).

problemStatement:
You are given a rooted tree with `n` nodes, each holding a value. Support many queries of the form:

1. ***pathQuery(u, v)*** — aggregate (e.g. sum or max) of the values on the path from `u` to `v`.
2. ***update(node, val)*** — change the value at a node.

The tree's shape is fixed. Use heavy-light decomposition with a segment tree so each path query runs in ***O(log² n)*** and each update in ***O(log n)***.
constraints: Up to 10⁵ interleaved pathQuery and update calls
The tree is rooted and its shape does not change
Aggregate is associative (sum, max, min, gcd); values fit in 64-bit
understanding: Subtree problems flatten cleanly with an Euler tour, but a path between two arbitrary nodes is not contiguous in DFS order. HLD fixes this by cutting the tree into chains along 'heavy' edges (toward the largest child) and laying each chain contiguously. The decomposition guarantees any root-to-node path touches only O(log n) chains, so a path becomes O(log n) contiguous ranges — exactly what a segment tree handles.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the queries on paths or subtrees?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Paths between two nodes. If they were subtree queries, an Euler tour with a Fenwick tree would be simpler and one log factor faster.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are values on nodes or edges?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Nodes here. Edge-valued variants assign each edge to its deeper endpoint and exclude the LCA from the final segment — a common off-by-one to call out.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the tree change shape?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. HLD assumes a fixed structure; the positions and chains are precomputed. Dynamic trees need link-cut trees.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How deep can recursion go?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to n on a chain. The two setup DFS passes should be iterative (explicit stack) so a 10⁵-deep tree does not overflow the call stack.

approaches.name: Baseline — Walk the Path via the LCA
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first: it is the obvious correct method and shows why long paths force a smarter layout.
hints: Find the LCA of u and v, then walk u up to the LCA and v up to the LCA, aggregating values along the way.
update(node, val) is one assignment — O(1).
A path can be the whole height of the tree, so a query is O(n). With many queries this is too slow — motivating a layout where a path is a few contiguous ranges.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Walking both halves of the path visits up to O(n) nodes (e.g. a chain). Updates are O(1). With q queries the cost is O(q·n).
approaches.explanation:
The direct method needs only parent pointers, depths, and per-node values.

**Find the meeting point.** Compute `lca(u, v)`. The path from `u` to `v` is `u → … → lca → … → v`.

**Walk and aggregate.** Step `u` upward to the LCA, combining each node's value; do the same for `v`; include the LCA once. The combine is whatever the query asks (sum, max, …).

**Why it is correct.** Every node on the `u`-to-`v` path is on one of the two upward walks to their LCA, and the LCA is the single shared top.

**Why it is too slow.** A path can span the entire height of the tree — O(n) for a chain. Answering 10⁵ such queries is O(n·q). The remedy is to relabel nodes so that the path decomposes into a *few* contiguous ranges that a segment tree aggregates in logarithmic time — which is exactly what HLD provides.
approaches.insight: The path-via-LCA walk is the conceptual baseline HLD accelerates: HLD keeps the same 'climb toward the LCA' motion but jumps a whole chain at a time (one segment-tree range) instead of one node at a time.

approaches.name: Heavy-Light Decomposition + Segment Tree (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for many path queries. 'Cut the tree into heavy chains, lay them contiguously, and a path becomes O(log n) segment-tree ranges.'

complexity.time: O(n) build, O(log² n) path query, O(log n) update

hints: First DFS: compute each node's subtree size and mark its heavy child (the child with the largest subtree). Heavy edges chain nodes together.

Second DFS: walk heavy children first so a chain's nodes get consecutive positions pos[node]; record head[node] = the top of the chain node belongs to. Build a segment tree over the base array indexed by pos.

Path query: while u and v are on different chains, take the segment-tree range for the deeper head's chain, then jump to parent[head] of that chain; once on the same chain, combine the final in-chain range. Each jump crosses one light edge, and there are at most O(log n) of those.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Both build DFS passes are O(n); building the segment tree is O(n). A path query crosses O(log n) chains (the light-edge bound), and each chain contributes one segment-tree range query costing O(log n) → O(log² n) per path query. A point update is one segment-tree update → O(log n).
approaches.explanation:
Heavy-light decomposition relabels the tree so that arbitrary paths become a few contiguous ranges, then lets a segment tree do the aggregation.

**Step 1 — choose heavy edges (why subtree size).** For each node, its *heavy child* is the child with the largest subtree; the edge to it is a *heavy edge*, every other child edge is *light*. The reason for picking by subtree size is the crucial guarantee: when you descend a light edge from a node, the child's subtree is at most half the parent's (otherwise that child would have been the heavy one). Halving can happen at most `log₂ n` times along any downward path, so **any root-to-node path crosses at most O(log n) light edges** — equivalently, it passes through at most O(log n) heavy chains.

**Step 2 — lay chains contiguously.** A *chain* is a maximal run of heavy edges. In a second DFS we always recurse into the heavy child *first*, assigning positions `pos[node]` in visit order. This makes every chain occupy a contiguous block of positions, and we record `head[node]` = the topmost node of the chain containing `node`. We then build a segment tree over the base array where index `pos[node]` holds `node`'s value.

**Step 3 — answer a path query.** To aggregate the path `u … v`, repeatedly look at the chain heads. While `head[u] ≠ head[v]`, the two nodes are on different chains: pick whichever has the *deeper* head (say `u`), aggregate the contiguous range `[pos[head[u]], pos[u]]` from the segment tree (the whole portion of `u`'s chain from its head down to `u`), then hop to the chain above by setting `u = parent[head[u]]`. Each hop crosses exactly one light edge, so this loop runs O(log n) times. When `head[u] == head[v]` the nodes are finally on the same chain; aggregate the single range between them (`[pos[deeper], pos[shallower]]`) and combine. The deeper-head node is implicitly the LCA's chain.

**Why O(log² n).** O(log n) chains, each costing an O(log n) segment-tree range query → O(log² n). Updates touch one position, so they are a plain O(log n) segment-tree update.

**Node vs edge values.** With values on nodes, include the LCA's position in the final same-chain range. With values on edges, store each edge's value at its deeper endpoint and *exclude* the LCA from that last range (`pos[lca] + 1` instead of `pos[lca]`) so the edge above the LCA is not wrongly added — the standard HLD off-by-one.

**How it relates to other tools.** The Euler tour makes *subtrees* contiguous; HLD makes *paths* (in pieces) contiguous. Binary lifting answers LCA alone. HLD is the heavyweight when you need aggregates along paths under updates.
approaches.insight: The entire power comes from one combinatorial fact: choosing the largest-subtree child as heavy forces light edges to be rare (≤ log n on any path). Rarity of light edges is what bounds the number of contiguous ranges a path decomposes into — and contiguous ranges are exactly what segment trees love. HLD is 'make the expensive thing (changing chains) rare, then reuse array structures'.

dryRun.intro: Subtree sizes: 0→5,1→3,2→1,3→1,4→1. Heavy child of 0 is 1, of 1 is 3 (tie broken to 3). Chains: {0,1,3} and {2},{4}. Path 3→4 has LCA 1.

code.python:
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

class HLD:
    def __init__(self, n: int, root: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int]], values: list[int]) -> None:
        self.n = n
        self.adj = defaultdict(list)
        for a, b in edges:
            self.adj[a].append(b)
            self.adj[b].append(a)
        self.parent = [root] * n
        self.depth = [0] * n
        self.heavy = [-1] * n
        self.size = [0] * n
        self.head = [0] * n
        self.pos = [0] * n
        self.timer = 0
        self.seg = [0] * (4 * n)

        self._dfs_size(root)
        self._decompose(root, root)
        base = [0] * n
        for v in range(n):
            base[self.pos[v]] = values[v]
        self._build(base, 1, 0, n - 1)

    def _dfs_size(self, root: int) -> None:
        order = []
        seen = [False] * self.n
        stack = [root]
        seen[root] = True
        while stack:                       # discovery order
            node = stack.pop()
            order.append(node)
            for nxt in self.adj[node]:
                if not seen[nxt]:
                    seen[nxt] = True
                    self.parent[nxt] = node
                    self.depth[nxt] = self.depth[node] + 1
                    stack.append(nxt)
        for node in reversed(order):       # children before parents
            self.size[node] = 1
            best, best_size = -1, 0
            for c in self.adj[node]:
                if c != self.parent[node]:
                    self.size[node] += self.size[c]
                    if self.size[c] > best_size:
                        best_size, best = self.size[c], c
            self.heavy[node] = best

    def _decompose(self, root: int, h: int) -> None:
        stack = [(root, h)]                # (node, chain head)
        while stack:
            node, chain_head = stack.pop()
            self.head[node] = chain_head
            self.pos[node] = self.timer
            self.timer += 1
            for c in self.adj[node]:       # light children start new chains
                if c != self.parent[node] and c != self.heavy[node]:
                    stack.append((c, c))
            if self.heavy[node] != -1:     # heavy child continues this chain
                stack.append((self.heavy[node], chain_head))

    def _build(self, base: list[int], node: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> None:
        if lo == hi:
            self.seg[node] = base[lo]; return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        self._build(base, 2 * node, lo, mid)
        self._build(base, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi)
        self.seg[node] = self.seg[2 * node] + self.seg[2 * node + 1]

    def _seg_update(self, node: int, lo: int, hi: int, i: int, v: int) -> None:
        if lo == hi:
            self.seg[node] = v; return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if i <= mid:
            self._seg_update(2 * node, lo, mid, i, v)
        else:
            self._seg_update(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, i, v)
        self.seg[node] = self.seg[2 * node] + self.seg[2 * node + 1]

    def _seg_query(self, node: int, lo: int, hi: int, l: int, r: int) -> int:
        if r < lo or hi < l:
            return 0
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:
            return self.seg[node]
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        return (self._seg_query(2 * node, lo, mid, l, r)
                + self._seg_query(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, l, r))

    def update(self, node: int, v: int) -> None:
        self._seg_update(1, 0, self.n - 1, self.pos[node], v)

    def path_query(self, u: int, v: int) -> int:
        res = 0
        while self.head[u] != self.head[v]:        # O(log n) chain hops
            if self.depth[self.head[u]] < self.depth[self.head[v]]:
                u, v = v, u
            res += self._seg_query(1, 0, self.n - 1, self.pos[self.head[u]], self.pos[u])
            u = self.parent[self.head[u]]
        if self.depth[u] > self.depth[v]:
            u, v = v, u
        res += self._seg_query(1, 0, self.n - 1, self.pos[u], self.pos[v])
        return res

edgeCases.behavior: Same chain immediately; the final range is [pos[node], pos[node]] → the node's own value.
Everything is one heavy chain; any path is a single contiguous range — HLD degenerates to a plain segment-tree range query.
Store edge values at the deeper endpoint and use pos[lca] + 1 for the final range so the edge above the LCA is excluded.

pitfalls: Choosing the heavy child by depth or degree instead of subtree size — loses the O(log n) light-edge bound.
Not visiting the heavy child first in DFS 2 — chains stop being contiguous and ranges break.
Double-counting or omitting the LCA in the final same-chain range (especially for edge values).
Recursive setup on a deep chain — stack overflow; build the two DFS passes iteratively.

commonMistakes: Selecting the heavy child by something other than largest subtree size.
Laying chains non-contiguously, so a chain is not a single segment-tree range.
Mishandling the LCA in the final same-chain segment (double-count or off-by-one for edges).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong heavy-child rule
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The O(log n) bound on light edges holds ONLY because the heavy child has the largest subtree, forcing every light edge to at least halve the remaining subtree. Picking by depth or first-child breaks the guarantee and paths can touch O(n) chains.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Heavy child not visited first
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Contiguous chains require the heavy child to receive the next consecutive position. If light children are positioned in between, a chain's nodes are scattered and a single segment-tree range no longer covers the chain.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: LCA handling in the final segment
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For node values the LCA must be counted once — include pos[lca]. For edge values it must be excluded — use pos[lca] + 1 — or you add the edge above the LCA that is not on the path.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# edge-valued tree, but including the LCA position:
res += self._seg_query(1, 0, self.n - 1, self.pos[u], self.pos[v])
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# edge-valued tree: skip the LCA's own position
res += self._seg_query(1, 0, self.n - 1, self.pos[u] + 1, self.pos[v])

followupVariations.hint: Swap the segment tree for one with lazy propagation; decompose the path the same way and range-add each chain segment.

followupVariations.hint: HLD's pos ordering also makes each subtree contiguous (pos[node] .. pos[node] + size[node] − 1), so one segment tree serves both.

followupVariations.title: Euler Tour of a Tree
followupVariations.hint: If you only need subtree queries, the simpler Euler tour + Fenwick tree is one log factor faster.

followupVariations.hint: When you only need the LCA or distance (no aggregates), lifting is shorter than full HLD.

patternNote: Heavy-light decomposition: mark the largest-subtree child of each node as heavy, lay the resulting chains contiguously, and back the array with a segment tree. Because light edges are at most O(log n) on any path, a path splits into O(log n) contiguous chain ranges, giving O(log² n) path queries and O(log n) updates. The standard tool for path aggregates with updates on a static-shape tree.
